sections.title: Foundations (Stages 1–3)
sections.description: Early computing ideas from Stages 1 to 3 — computers around us, clear instructions and staying safe.

questions.question: In a game program, the player’s score is kept in a variable. What is a variable?
questions.options: A named space in a program that stores a value that can change | A message sent across a network | A picture that a sprite wears | A block that makes the program repeat forever
questions.correctAnswer: A named space in a program that stores a value that can change
questions.explanation: A variable is like a labelled box inside the program. The score lives in the box, and the program can change what is inside while it runs.

questions.question: Layla wants to build a quiz game. First she splits the big job into smaller jobs: draw the screens, write the questions, keep the score. Which computational thinking skill is she using?
questions.options: Repetition | Selection | Debugging | Decomposition
questions.explanation: Decomposition means breaking a big problem into smaller parts. Each small part is easier to plan and build than the whole game at once.

questions.question: A program says: IF the answer is correct THEN add 1 to the score, ELSE show a hint. What is this kind of choosing called?
questions.options: Selection | An output | Repetition | A variable
questions.explanation: Selection is when a program tests a condition and chooses between different paths — IF this is true, do one thing, ELSE do another.

questions.question: A program starts with score = 4. Then it runs the instruction: score = score + 3. What is the value of score now?
questions.explanation: The instruction takes the old value of score, which is 4, adds 3 to it, and puts the answer back: 4 + 3 = 7.

questions.question: Before building her program, Amina writes a list of everything it must do to count as finished and working. What is this list called?
questions.options: A database | Success criteria | An IP address | A bug report
questions.explanation: Success criteria are the list of things a program must do to be a success. Amina can tick each one off as she tests her program.

questions.question: Bilal’s program should count from 1 to 10, but it stops at 9. He reads his code, finds the mistake and fixes it. What is this process called?
questions.options: Downloading | Debugging | Decomposing | Charting
questions.explanation: Finding and fixing mistakes in a program is called debugging. Every programmer does it — a bug is a clue, not a failure.

questions.question: Which of these is continuous data?
questions.options: The mass of a school bag | A learner’s favourite colour | The number of pets in a family | The name of a town
questions.correctAnswer: The mass of a school bag
questions.explanation: Continuous data is measured and can take any value in between, like 2.4 kg or 2.45 kg. Counts and names are not continuous.

questions.question: In a spreadsheet, which of these is written correctly as a formula that adds cells B2 and B3?
questions.options: ADD B2 AND B3 | B2+B3= | +B2B3 | =B2+B3
questions.explanation: Every spreadsheet formula begins with an equals sign, so the software knows to calculate. =B2+B3 adds whatever is in those two cells.

questions.question: Cell D2 holds the formula =B2*C2. What happens if the number in cell B2 is changed?
questions.options: C2 changes to match B2 | The formula in D2 is deleted | The result in D2 updates automatically | Nothing changes until the file is printed
questions.correctAnswer: The result in D2 updates automatically
questions.explanation: A formula uses cell references, not fixed numbers. Change one cell and every formula that uses it recalculates by itself — that is the power of a spreadsheet.

questions.question: Halima measured the temperature every hour for a whole day. Which chart shows best how it changed over time?
questions.options: A single bar | A pie chart | A list of names | A line graph
questions.explanation: A line graph joins the measurements in time order, so you can see the temperature rising and falling across the day.

questions.question: A plain list says: 7, 9, 10. With labels it says: Aden scored 7, Sara scored 9, Omar scored 10. What has the plain data been turned into?
questions.options: Hardware | Information | An algorithm | A network
questions.explanation: Data is raw facts on their own. When data is organised and given meaning — like whose score each number is — it becomes information.

questions.question: Which device joins a home network to the internet?
questions.options: A printer | A router | A mouse | A monitor
questions.explanation: The router is the doorway of the network: it passes data between the devices at home and the wider internet.

questions.question: Before a photo travels across the internet, it is broken into small pieces that travel separately and are put back together at the other end. What are these pieces called?
questions.options: Folders | Packets | Passwords | Pixels
questions.explanation: Data travels the internet in packets. Each packet can take its own route, and the receiving computer puts them back together in order.

questions.question: Why do people type a website name, like a URL, instead of the site’s IP address?
questions.options: Names are easier for people to remember than long numbers | Typing a name makes the internet run faster | Websites do not really have IP addresses | Numbers cannot travel through cables
questions.correctAnswer: Names are easier for people to remember than long numbers
questions.explanation: Every website has an IP address made of numbers, but people remember words far more easily — so we type the name and the computer looks up the number.

questions.question: During an online lesson, the school’s internet connection fails. Which of these can the learners still do on their computers?
questions.options: Send an email to another school | Watch a live video stream | Open a file saved on the computer itself | Load a brand-new web page
questions.correctAnswer: Open a file saved on the computer itself
questions.explanation: When the internet fails, only jobs that need the network stop. A file stored on the computer itself does not need the internet, so it still opens.

questions.question: A stranger in an online game chat asks for your home address. What should you do?
questions.options: Share it only if they ask twice | Ask the stranger for their address first | Share it if the stranger seems friendly | Do not share it and tell a trusted adult
questions.correctAnswer: Do not share it and tell a trusted adult
questions.explanation: Your address is personal information, and it stays private online — always. Telling a trusted adult keeps you and other players safe.

questions.question: Which of these is an input device?
questions.options: A printer | A microphone | A screen | A speaker
questions.explanation: Input goes INTO the computer. A microphone carries sound in; speakers, printers and screens all send information out.

questions.question: In an automatic door, a sensor notices a person coming. What is the motor that then pushes the door open called?
questions.options: A browser | A spreadsheet | A password | An actuator
questions.explanation: An actuator is a special output device that gives out movement instead of pictures or sound — like the motor that opens the door.

questions.question: Deep inside a computer, all data is stored using only two digits. Which two?
questions.options: 2 and 10 | 1 and 2 | 1 and 0 | 0 and 9
questions.explanation: Computers store everything with tiny on/off switches. On is written as 1 and off as 0 — these are the binary digits.

questions.question: A phone keyboard guesses your next word while you type. Which computing idea is this an everyday example of?
questions.options: A network cable | A storage device | A paper database | Artificial intelligence
questions.explanation: Predictive text is a simple form of artificial intelligence: the phone learns from lots of writing to guess which word is likely to come next.

questions.question: In Scratch, which block makes a dance animation repeat again and again without ever stopping on its own?
questions.options: when clicked | wait | say | forever
questions.explanation: The forever block is a loop that never stops by itself — perfect for an animation that keeps dancing until you stop the program.

questions.question: To draw a square, a repeat loop runs the steps 'move forward, then turn 90 degrees'. How many times must the loop repeat?
questions.explanation: A square has 4 sides and 4 corners, so the loop repeats the move-and-turn steps 4 times — once for each side.

questions.question: What is an algorithm?
questions.options: A kind of internet cable | A part of a computer you can touch | A set of clear steps in the right order for doing a task | A game with no rules
questions.correctAnswer: A set of clear steps in the right order for doing a task
questions.explanation: An algorithm is a recipe for a task: clear steps, in the right order. Robots and programs only work because someone wrote them a good algorithm.

questions.question: A data table lists the members of a reading club, one member per row. What is each row of the table called?
questions.options: A pixel | A formula | A record | A field
questions.explanation: In a data table, each row is a record — all the information about one member. Each column is a field, one kind of information.

questions.question: On a school network, one computer stores the shared files and hands them out when other computers ask. What is this computer called?
questions.options: A server | A client | A sensor | A keyboard
questions.explanation: A server gives things out — files, printing, web pages. The computers that ask for them are the clients.

questions.question: A secret code swaps every letter for the letter 3 places later in the alphabet, so A becomes D. What does B become?
questions.options: F | E | A | C
questions.explanation: Count 3 letters on from B: C, D, E. So B becomes E. This letter-shifting code is called a Caesar cipher.

questions.question: A robot vacuum cleaner is a control system that works in three steps. Which order is correct?
questions.options: Sense, think, act | Act, sense, think | Sense, act, think | Think, act, sense
questions.explanation: A control system first senses the world with its inputs, then its processor thinks about what to do, and finally it acts — like turning away from a wall.

questions.question: On a micro:bit light show, one loop runs exactly 5 times and another runs over and over without stopping. Which pair names them correctly?
questions.options: repeat (5) counts and stops; forever never stops on its own | forever counts to five; repeat (5) never stops | Both loops always stop after five turns | Both loops run without ever stopping
questions.correctAnswer: repeat (5) counts and stops; forever never stops on its own
questions.explanation: repeat (5) is count-controlled: it runs five times, then stops. forever keeps going until the program is stopped — great for twinkling light art.

questions.question: Which of these is a computer you might find at home?
questions.options: A wooden spoon | A tablet | A paper book | A pillow
questions.explanation: A tablet is a computer: it follows instructions, shows things on a screen and responds when you tap it. Computers are all around us.

questions.question: You are writing instructions for making a jam sandwich. Which step must come FIRST?
questions.options: Get two slices of bread | Put the sandwich on a plate | Press the slices together | Eat the sandwich
questions.explanation: Instructions only work in the right order. You cannot spread, press or eat anything until the bread is out first.

questions.question: Which everyday machine has a small computer inside that follows instructions?
questions.options: A glass of water | A washing machine | A cotton T-shirt | A garden rock
questions.explanation: A washing machine has a tiny computer inside. When you choose a wash program, the computer follows its instructions step by step.

questions.question: Which of these is safe to share in a public online post?
questions.options: Your favourite animal | Your home address | Your school’s name and class | Your parent’s phone number
questions.explanation: Things that help a stranger find you — your address, school or phone numbers — stay private. A favourite animal gives nothing away.

questions.question: A friend’s program has its steps in the wrong order, so it does not do what they planned. What should your friend do?
questions.options: Put the steps in the correct order and test it again | Ask the computer to guess the order | Add extra steps at the end | Keep running it and hope it changes
questions.correctAnswer: Put the steps in the correct order and test it again
questions.explanation: A program only does what its steps say, in the order they are written. Fix the order, run it again, and check it does what you planned.

questions.question: What is a network?
questions.options: A single computer with nothing connected to it | Computers and devices joined together so they can share things | A drawing of a spider’s web on paper | A box for keeping pencils tidy
questions.correctAnswer: Computers and devices joined together so they can share things
questions.explanation: A network is computers and devices connected together so they can share files, printers and messages with each other.
